catalog_quote: This paper proposes an orthography for Naami, a Beboid language spoken in the North West Region of Cameroon, Donga-Mantung division, Misaje subdivision. Like other Bantoid languages, Naami is a tonal language, spoken by about 4,400 people as stated in the Ethnologue (2021). ... [sec. 3.1 Basic Naami Tone, p. 17] Grace Tabah (2011) identified nine contrastive tones in Naami: three level tones (high, mid and low) and six contour tones (low-high, high-low, mid-low, mid-high, low-mid, and high-mid). Below are examples of words with the three level tones and the six contour tones: ... None of these nine contrastive lexical tones are consistently marked with diacritics (as in many Cameroonian languages outside of the Misaje area). ... [sec. 3.2, p. 18] Tone in Naami also plays important grammatical roles. For instance, the difference between certain singular and plural nouns (section 3.2.1), the difference between certain tenses (sections 3.2.2 and 3.2.3) and the difference between certain moods (section 3.2.4). ... [3.2.1] Like most Beboid languages, the only difference between class 9 and class 10 nouns in Naami is tone.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Naami/Bebe is described as a lexical and grammatical tone language (three level tones H/M/L plus six contours; tone distinguishes noun classes 9/10, P2/P3, F2/F3, hortative). Neither the orthography guide (the only accessible document with a phonology section) nor the 2020 sketch grammar says anything about word stress or accent: no placement rule, no statement that stress is absent.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement exists to have exceptions).
new_statements.domain_note: n/a for stress. Tone examples are citation-form monosyllables and nouns; vowel length is contrastive (sec.2.2.1).
new_statements.identity_note: All SIL Cameroon materials use the name Naami for Bebe [bzv] = bebe1250 (Glottolog has no dialect subcodes). The orthography guide names two dialects (bebe-kette / bebe-jato); the Webonary introduction says the Sabongida (Bebe-Jatto side) dialect was chosen for the New Testament and dictionary, so the described variety is Sabongida Naami. Cox 2005 (also saved) describes the sister language Kemedzung [dmo] keme1240, not Bebe, and was read for context only.
